Virtual memory is the cornerstone of modern operating system design, providing the illusion of a vast, contiguous pool of memory to applications while physically residing on slower storage devices. To understand how virtual memory, page faults, working sets, and memory-mapped files interact, one must view them not as isolated concepts, but as components of a dynamic feedback loop that governs system performance. This interaction is critical for developers aiming to write efficient software, as mismanagement of these elements can lead to severe performance degradation known as "thrashing."

At the lowest level, virtual memory allows the operating system to map virtual addresses used by a program to physical addresses in RAM or to disk storage. When a program accesses a virtual address, the Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates this address. If the corresponding data is already in physical RAM, the access is fast. However, if the data resides on the disk, the hardware triggers a **page fault**. A page fault is not an error; it is a signal to the operating system that the requested page must be fetched from secondary storage into physical memory. This process involves suspending the current process, locating the page on disk, finding a free frame in RAM (or evicting an existing page), reading the data, updating the page table,
